```cpp
#if PANDAS_HAVE_AVX512CD

```

with 

```cpp
if constexpr (kEnableAVX512CD) {
    ::add
}
```

But I don't think that matters much for the rest of the implementation

author: WillAyd
body:
Hmm OK thanks. I asked Claude about this pattern as I wasn't sure and got a seemingly credible response:

```cpp
The SIMD-specific reason (this is the big one)

  Different SIMD architectures require different compiler flags. To use AVX-512 intrinsics, the TU must be compiled with -mavx512f. To use AVX2, with -mavx2. Etc.

  If you instantiate batch in a header, that header gets compiled with whatever flags the including .cpp was compiled with. If moments.cpp is compiled with -mavx2 (or no SIMD
  flags), the AVX-512 intrinsics inside the template body either don't exist or are emulated badly — and you get exactly the kind of error you're seeing.

  The standard SIMD pattern is:

  moments_simd.hpp           — declarations + extern template
  moments_avx512f.cpp        — compiled with -mavx512f, instantiates avx512f version
  moments_avx2.cpp           — compiled with -mavx2,    instantiates avx2 version
  moments_sse2.cpp           — compiled with -msse2,    instantiates sse2 version
  moments_dispatch.cpp       — runtime CPU detect, calls the right one

  Each .cpp is built as a separate TU with its own flags. The header just declares "these instantiations exist somewhere" via extern template, and the linker stitches it together.
```

Is that what you are seeing here? I have seen that pattern before in say Arrow:

https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/main/cpp/src/arrow/util/bpacking_simd_internal.h

So happy to keep the extern, although I think we should follow the rest of the pattern and put each implementation into its own module with its own flags, rather than one moments.cpp

I can see where that is confusing - it looks like xsimd offers a xsimd::detail::supported type which can be used to filter an arch_list from a set of types to those that are actually supported. I'm not sure why that is in the detail namespace, but it appears to have the missing functionality.

You may want to ask upstream why that isn't public, and if there's a desire to make it so in the future. In the meantime you could still just use it, as its available in a header file.

Keep in mind that if you stick to that pattern, you can leverage other parts of the static type system for xsimd, like the `xsimd::arch_list::best`. Things like that are very difficult to represent with macros, so we want to implement design patterns that we will use consistently

Overall I feel like that is a much simpler solution, and it prevents us from maintaining bit fiddling code ourselves.

> Thanks for the example, I thought in using something like this, but again, it would rely on macros to define these `constexpr` variables, since [meson configuration](https://mesonbuild.com/Configuration.html) is designed to define macros.

You are correct that the config file is where this needs to be done, but I think are missing the way to do it. Essentially you would make the constexpr items live in an input template, which here can be `pandas_simd_config.h.in`. The contents would look something like:

```cpp
#pragma once

static constexpr bool kHasAVX2 = @PANDAS_HAVE_AVX2@;
static constexpr bool kHasSSE2 = @PANDAS_HAVE_SSE2@;
...
```

and then provide that input template as an argument to `configure_file`

```python
configure_file(
  input: 'pandas_simd_config.h.in',
  output: 'pandas_simd_config.h',
  ...
)
```

author: WillAyd
body:
> Meson's `configure_file` (like CMake's) is designed, mainly, to generate macro headers where keys can be left undefined.

This is a very common pattern with both Meson and CMake. The latter always requires you to specify a file like this. We just generating a header.

> The `std::conditional_t` approach in [#64905 (comment)](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64905#discussion_r3248748482) also adds complexity. Using `void` as a placeholder for unsupported architectures breaks `xsimd::dispatch`:

It looks like xsimd offers an `xsimd::unavailable` sentinel - if you use that in place of `void` in your example it will compile and run.

> Also, macros keep this configuration accessible to C and Cython, if necessary.

If you wanted to you could name this output .hpp to clarify that it is only used for C++ projects. I see what you are saying, but C / C++ are separate languages; discarding functionality of the latter for compatibility with the former is not worthwhile

> Even the [CppCoreGuidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#es31-dont-use-macros-for-constants-or-functions) allow for this:
> 
> > **Enforcement:** Scream when you see a macro that **isn’t just used for source control** (e.g., `#ifdef`)

This is exactly the problem. You are using macros when you are trying to control a type. Both xsimd and C++ offer robust compile time type manipulations that you are forgoing. 

> IMO, using template headers with `constexpr` for the sake of avoiding macros feels like sacrificing simplicity and portability without a concrete benefit.

How does this sacrifice portability? This is all part of the C++ standard.

I will never claim that C++ is a simple language. However, its features do exist for good reason

body: I think the `copy=False` cannot be used unconditionally here, for correct CoW behaviour. If `where` would always return a _hard_ copy, that would be fine, but `where` will detect "no-op" cases where it can return the input again.

author: jorisvandenbossche
body:
Example with how `Series.where` is correctly tracking this:

```python
>>> ser1 = pd.Series([1,2,3])
>>> ser2 = ser1.where([True]*3, 100)
# ser2 will share the data with ser1 
>>> ser2._references.has_reference()
True
# trying to update the series breaks that reference
>>> ser2[0] = 100
>>> ser2._references.has_reference()
False
# showing again, but mutating the underlying values to circumvent our CoW mechanism
>>> ser1 = pd.Series([1,2,3])
>>> ser2 = ser1.where([True]*3, 100)
>>> ser1.array[0] = 100
# also ser2 is updated
>>> ser2
0    100
1      2
2      3
dtype: int64
```

Similar example but now with Index, where the references are no longer correctly tracked:

```python
>>> idx1 = pd.Index([1,2,3])
>>> idx2 = idx1.where([True]*3, 100)
# this should be True
>>> idx2._references.has_reference()
False
# because the reference from idx2 to idx1 is not tracked, we can get 
# wrong CoW behaviour, eg here by converting idx2 to a series to make it mutable
>>> idx2 = pd.Series(idx2)
>>> idx2._references.has_reference()
False
>>> idx2[0] = 100
# original index should not be updated
>>> idx1
Index([100, 2, 3], dtype='int64')
```

The above is on main, while with 3.0 this behaves correctly

```
      expected = DataFrame(
          {
              "t": pd.DatetimeIndex(keys[join_type]).tz_convert("US/Eastern").as_unit("us"),
              "a": avals[join_type],
              "b": bvals[join_type],
          }
      )

      assert result["t"].dtype == left["t"].dtype
```

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex(
    levels=[["b", "a"], ["y", "x"]],
    codes=[[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1]],

)
s = pd.Series(range(4), index=mi)
res = s.unstack("L1").stack()

# L0  L1

#     x     1
# a   y     2
#     x     3
# dtype: int64
tm.assert_series_equal(res, res.sort_index())
```

Since `simd_config_inc` is only actually needed by `tokenizer.c`, we should avoid polluting the search path of other extensions. I think it's better to consolidate the `tokenizer.c` into a library, here is the patch with the idea:

```diff
diff --git a/pandas/_libs/meson.build b/pandas/_libs/meson.build
index 26f0d0c673..d1ca671c3d 100644

+++ b/pandas/_libs/meson.build
@@ -55,6 +55,20 @@ fast_float = subproject('fast_float')

 xsimd_dep = dependency('xsimd', version: '>=14.2')
 
+tokenizer_lib = static_library(
+    'pandas_tokenizer',
+    'src/parser/fast_float_strtod.cpp',
+    'src/parser/pd_strtoi.cpp',
+    'src/parser/tokenizer.c',
+    include_directories: [inc_pd, py.get_path('include'), simd_config_inc],
+    dependencies: [fast_float_dep],
+)
+
+tokenizer_dep = declare_dependency(
+    link_with: tokenizer_lib,
+    include_directories: [inc_pd],
+)
+
 subdir('simd')
 
 subdir('tslibs')
@@ -94,11 +108,8 @@ libs_sources = {
```

Instead of reusing fast_float_strtod, it should be better to specify which option do you want and use `from_chars_advanced`.

```c++
enum class chars_format : uint64_t {
  scientific = 1 << 0,
  fixed = 1 << 2,
  hex = 1 << 3,
  no_infnan = 1 << 4,
  // RFC 8259: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8259#section-6
  json = uint64_t(detail::basic_json_fmt) | fixed | scientific | no_infnan,
  // Extension of RFC 8259 where, e.g., "inf" and "nan" are allowed.
  json_or_infnan = uint64_t(detail::basic_json_fmt) | fixed | scientific,
  fortran = uint64_t(detail::basic_fortran_fmt) | fixed | scientific,
  general = fixed | scientific,
  allow_leading_plus = 1 << 7,
  skip_white_space = 1 << 8,
};
```

With this, you should be able to avoid having to parse the beggining `start`

Here is a patch with the idea:

```suggestion
var_a = np.dot(a, a)
if var_a == 0:
    return np.nan
    
var_b = np.dot(b, b)
if var_b == 0:
    return np.nan

cov_ab = np.dot(a, b)

coef_det = (cov_ab / var_a) * (cov_ab / var_b)
r_abs = np.sqrt(coef_det)
result = -r_abs if cov_ab < 0 else r_abs

return np.clip(result, -1.0, 1.0)
```

author: jorisvandenbossche
body:
Speaking as a pandas maintainer, I agree with @xmatthias that there is definitely value in keeping Feather / Arrow IPC file support around. 

The _file format_ that pandas writes and reads is not deprecated at all, and it is indeed only a matter of interface and naming. We could have a discussion whether we want to preserve the current "feather" naming in pandas, or also move towards the naming that Arrow now uses, but that's something else as just plain deprecating the current function.

> It isn’t a “change a line of code to use the same function in a new place” change, it’s “re-implement and maintain a bunch of wrapping logic”.

I don't think there is much of "maintain a bunch of wrapping logic" involved here (not much more to maintain than we currently have to do). It is true that the replacement in pyarrow is not exactly a new 1-liner for the existing `pyarrow.feather.write_feather`/`pyarrow.feather.read_table` (because the way the IPC interface works, it will require multiple lines). But it is mostly still a one-time update.

body:
Finally had the time to give this a proper look .. I didn't check all prior review rounds and comments, so apologies in advance if I repeat something that already has been discussed before (please point out if so, I don't necessarily want to reopen past items).

And thanks for all the effort here!

Apart from the inline comments, a few questions:

- For numeric EAs (and in case you don't need a custom converter, like you do have in astropy with the units), you only need to define the `ExtensionDtype._is_numeric` attribute to have plotting working? (about which this PR changed nothing I suppose, but just verifying to understand the full picture of EA plotting)
- Suppose you want to have an EA plottable but which gets converted to data that matplotlib already can handle fine, then it is just pandas that will not consider it "plottable" out of the box? But then to have it plottable, you have to return something from the `_get_plot_converter`, while you don't actually have a converter to register. 
  - Now, in practice this might only be the case for `decimal` right now (or `str`, but that is clearly something to fix in pandas), because whenever your data converts to numeric data, you are in the case from above and you can ensure pandas considers it plottable by defining `_is_numeric` (and I don't think matplotlib supports anything else out of the box, apart from date(time) which we already register as plottable as well)
- Should we include (i.e. consider as plottable) anything that is in `matplotlib.units.registry`?
- For actual custom types, this currently relies on matplotlib calling `converter.convert()` on each value in a for-loop, is that right? A possible future enhancement would be to allow the EA also provide the "numeric data to plot" (the EA might be able to do this a lot faster)?

For testing, it would be nice to implement a custom `_get_plot_converter` in one of the test extension arrays to have coverage for this (the only `_get_plot_converter` in the PR right now is the one on DatetimeTZDtype, and that is also a bit a special case handled specifically in timeseries plotting machinery, I assume? i.e. I would think this does not actually go through `converter.convert()` when making a line plot?) 
(I was thinking DecimalArray would be a good one, but that one already works because of being numeric, I suppose)

The reason I made the suggestion here is because it stood out to me. We certainly don't need to have the text flow until the full end of our max line length, I don't mind that (and so we certainly don't need strict linting rules or so for this). 
But line length (at least in the verbatim text case of the docstring, this is of course not an issue for the rendered html one) does have _some_ semantic meaning. Like you might expect that a sentence ends if it stops much shorter than the rest of the paragraph (or that a full paragraph consists of lines that are more or less the same length). And if it deviates enough it cause some "noise" in the reading experience is my feeling. At least here it caught my attention, and ideally it doesn't.

Long text to try to explain why I made the suggestion ;)

author: Alvaro-Kothe
body:
> CPython [reads](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/9eaf48a56547872b86de5cecbaa7edd3279159ed/Objects/object.c#L774) tp->tp_hash directly

CPython can access those fields directly because it is the interpreter itself. External extensions should be bound by their compatibility rules.

My concern is that `PyTypeObject` is an [opaque struct](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/type.html#c.PyTypeObject), so acessing its members directly may cause some problems in the future. I think the correct way to acess its members is with [PyType_GetSlot](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/type.html#c.PyType_GetSlot).

I think this is the safer way to acess its slot:

```suggestion
  hashfunc tp_hash_slot = (hashfunc)PyType_GetSlot(tp, Py_tp_hash);
  return tp_hash_slot != NULL && tp_hash_slot != PyObject_HashNotImplemented;
```

author: rhshadrach
body:
With

```python
is_replaced = np.zeros(self.shape[0], dtype=bool)
for locs, _ in pieces:
    is_replaced[locs] = True
```

I think we can simplify and speed this up.

```python
blocks = []
for blk in self.blocks:
    # Keep each run of adjacent kept columns within a block as one view.
    mgr_locs = blk.mgr_locs.as_array
    kept = np.concatenate([[False], ~is_replaced[mgr_locs], [False]])
    bounds = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(kept))
    for start, end in zip(bounds[::2], bounds[1::2], strict=True):
        blocks.append(
            blk.getitem_block_columns(
                slice(start, end), BlockPlacement(mgr_locs[start:end])
            )
        )
```
